name: SkinPen
lead: SkinPen is a handheld microneedling pen used by clinicians for collagen induction therapy, a cosmetic procedure in which tiny sterile needles repeatedly puncture the skin. People use it to improve the look of acne scars and skin texture.[1]

Microneedling is also called skin needling or dermarolling, and has been used for scarring and acne; some studies suggest it combined with minoxidil may help hair loss more than minoxidil alone.[1] SkinPen is marketed as a cleared medical microneedling device. Separately, a 2023 paper uses the name "SkinPen" for an unrelated handheld wound-healing bioprinter in rats.[2]

chain: Skin responds with repair and collagen
angle.text: Controlled micro-injuries prompt the skin to rebuild, which people use to soften acne scars and roughness over a series of sessions.

paras: Collagen induction therapy punctures the skin with many tiny sterile needles. It differs from microneedling used for drug or vaccine delivery.[1]
Microneedling is discussed for scars and skin quality, and in combination with minoxidil for hair. Treatments combined with platelet-rich plasma are described as unproven pending studies.[1]

Health officials have warned that PRP-combined microneedling "vampire facials" given in non-medical settings without infection control carry risks of blood-borne infection; in April 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses linked to one New Mexico spa.[1]

No studies found. A 2023 paper uses the name SkinPen for a different device, a wound-healing bioprinter, tested in diabetic rats.[2] A pilot study on androgenetic alopecia reported benefits of microneedling generally.[1]

card.summary: A clinician-used microneedling pen that makes tiny skin punctures to help smooth acne scars and texture.
card.note: Use in non-clinical settings has been linked to infection reports.

quick.overview:
SkinPen is a handheld microneedling device. It makes many tiny punctures that prompt the skin to repair itself.

People use it for acne scars and rougher skin texture, usually in repeated sessions.
quick.mechanism: Fine sterile needles create controlled micro-injuries; the skin responds by remodeling and producing collagen.
quick.risks: Infection risk rises when done without proper hygiene; officials have warned about spa treatments, especially with blood-based add-ons.
